screens.title: Getting Started with Python
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this short course you will learn how to install Python, interact with the interpreter, and run your first program. We start with the practical step of getting a trusted installer and making sure the operating system can find Python by adding it to PATH. Then you will try the interactive interpreter, called the REPL, to get immediate feedback and verify basic expressions and the print function. Finally you will create and run a small script file to see how script mode differs from interactive mode. Along the way I’ll show you common starter errors like a missing parenthesis or a misspelled function name and how to read the interpreter’s messages to fix them. A concrete example you will use is creating hello dot P Y file that prints two lines to the terminal and running it with the python command. This matters because a correct installation and basic workflow let you move from experimenting to building programs reliably. As you follow along, notice the commands and the error messages, and ask yourself: after installing, can I run python and pip from any directory? That ability is the most important indicator your setup is ready.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical, verifiable skills. First, you will be able to install Python and ensure the operating system can invoke it from any folder. This matters because a correct install is the foundation for running code and installing packages. Second, you will be able to explain what the Python interpreter is and use interactive mode to experiment quickly. Interactive mode helps you test ideas before committing them to a file. Third, you will write, save, and execute a simple Python script file from the terminal so you can move from experiments to reproducible runs. Finally, you will recognize and fix common startup errors such as a missing parenthesis or a misspelled function name. For each objective you will see a short demonstration and a small milestone you can check off, so you have concrete evidence of skill growth. These four outcomes prepare you to move on to variables, data types, and simple programs with confidence.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Practice Plan

Short Drills

A set of verifiable steps you can complete in 10 minutes to confirm each skill.

Install & Verify
Run these commands after installing: python --version and pip --version. If either returns an error, check PATH or reinstall.
Interactive Check
Enter the interpreter, try arithmetic like 5 * 7, then call the print function to see output. Exit with exit() or the platform shortcut.
Script Run
Create my_first_script.py with two print calls, save, cd to the folder, and run python my_first_script.py to see both lines printed.
Troubleshoot
If you see SyntaxError or NameError, read the message, fix punctuation or typos, save, and re-run. The error message gives the likely location to inspect.

screens.title: Installing Python and the importance of PATH
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Python is the first technical step and a common source of friction for beginners. The installer provides the Python executable and pip, the package installer. It is important to use the official installer mentioned in this chapter to avoid altered distributions. One particularly critical option on Windows is the checkbox to add Python to PATH. PATH is an operating-system environment list of folders that the terminal searches for executables. When Python is added to PATH you can type the python command from any folder and the interpreter will launch. Without that setting you may see a "command not found" or similar error, which means the system cannot locate the python program. A concrete example: after installation you will run python --version and expect a version string. If you see an error, re-run the installer and enable adding to PATH, or update the PATH environment variable manually. A common misconception is that installation always 'just works'; in fact, small checkbox choices matter. Key takeaway: confirm install with python --version and pip --version before moving on — these two checks prove your environment can run code and install packages.

keyIdea.title: Add Python to PATH

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Install & PATH
Why PATH matters
  • PATH tells your terminal where to look for programs like python and pip.
  • Adding Python to PATH during installation allows simple commands like python --version to work anywhere.
  • If PATH is not set you will see an error when invoking python from a folder that doesn't contain the interpreter.
Verification commands
python --version pip --version
Pro Tip
On macOS and Linux you may use python3 instead of python if your system reserves python for another version.
Installation steps (general)
  1. Download the official installer referenced in this chapter.
  2. Run the installer. On Windows, enable "Add Python to PATH".
  3. Open a terminal and run the verification commands above.
Common mistake
Skipping the PATH checkbox on Windows or not using the correct command (python vs python3) causes a "command not found" error. Re-run the installer or update PATH to fix this.
Key Takeaway

Verify your install immediately with python --version and pip --version. If those succeed, move to the REPL test.

screens.title: What is the Python interpreter?
screens.narratorSegment: The Python interpreter is the executable that reads your Python statements, translates them into operations, and performs them. Think of the interpreter as a translator that reads each line you write and does what you ask. There are two common ways to use the interpreter: interactive mode and script mode. In interactive mode you type a line and the interpreter responds immediately; this is ideal for testing ideas and learning syntax. In script mode you save a sequence of commands into a dot P Y file file and ask the interpreter to run the whole file from top to bottom. A concrete example of the interpreter in action is entering the REPL and typing a simple arithmetic expression; the interpreter evaluates it and returns the result. A common misconception is to confuse the interpreter with an editor: the interpreter executes code, while an editor simply stores it. To confirm the interpreter is available, run python --version. If the command prints the version, the interpreter is ready. Now consider how you will use interactive mode to experiment before writing scripts: that flow saves time when learning new concepts.

keyIdea.title: Interpreter = executor
keyIdea.text: The interpreter executes code either interactively or by running a script file.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Interpreter
Python Interpreter

A program that reads and executes Python code. It supports two modes: interactive REPL and running scripts saved in files.

Interactive Mode (REPL)
Type commands, see immediate results, useful for quick tests and learning syntax.
Script Mode
Save code in a .py file and run the file as a program to produce repeatable output.
Quick example
$ python >>> 2 + 2 4 >>> print("Hello, Cohortia!") Hello, Cohortia!
Analogy
The interpreter is like a radio host who reads scripts (your code) and performs actions for listeners (the computer). Interactive mode is like improvisation; script mode is reading a prepared piece.
Key Takeaway

Use the REPL to test ideas quickly, then move working code into scripts for repeatable runs.

screens.title: Using the interactive REPL
screens.narratorSegment: The interactive Read-Eval-Print Loop, or REPL, is where you type a Python expression and the interpreter evaluates it immediately. This is an ideal environment when you want to confirm syntax or test a small idea. To enter interactive mode type python or Python three in the terminal and press Enter. You will see the >>> prompt. At that prompt you can type arithmetic like 5 * 7 and press Enter to get the result. You can also call the print function to display text. For example, calling the print function with a greeting shows that the interpreter outputs strings correctly. When you are done, exit the REPL by calling exit() or using the platform-specific shortcut, such as Ctrl+D on Mac O S and Linux, or Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows. A common misconception is that work typed into the REPL is automatically saved; it is not. Use the REPL to experiment and then move the tested lines into a script file to preserve your work. Try a short sequence: start Python, compute a quick calculation, print a message, and then exit. That flow builds confidence and confirms the interpreter executes code as expected.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Interactive REPL
Enter and use the REPL
Type python or python3 and press Enter. Look for the >>> prompt, then type expressions or call the print function to see results instantly.
$ python >>> 100 / 3 33.333333333333336 >>> print("My first interactive Python line!") My first interactive Python line!
Exit with exit(), Ctrl+D (macOS/Linux), or Ctrl+Z then Enter (Windows).
Practice prompts
  • Compute 5 * 7 and confirm the numeric result.
  • Call the print function with a short message to verify string output.
  • Try a quick type error to see an interpreter message and learn how it looks.
Common Mistake
Expecting the REPL to save work. Lines typed here disappear when you exit. Save important code in a file instead.
Key Takeaway

Use the REPL to test expressions quickly, then copy successful lines into a script for reuse.

screens.title: Create and run your first Python script
screens.narratorSegment: Writing your first script turns interactive trials into a reproducible program. Open a simple text editor and create a file named hello dot P Y file. Inside the file put two lines that call the print function to display messages. Save the file in a folder you can find easily, for example a projects folder or the Desktop. Then open your terminal and navigate to that folder using the cd command. Once you are in the correct folder, run the script by typing python hello dot P Y file or Python three hello dot P Y file depending on your system. You will see the two lines printed in order. A concrete script example from this chapter prints a friendly greeting and a short sentence about Python being fun. A common misconception is to expect the editor to run the file automatically; you must invoke the interpreter from the terminal. If the output does not appear, confirm you saved the file and that you are in the same directory. This simple flow — edit, save, cd, run — is a foundational loop you will repeat often.

keyIdea.title: Edit → Save → Run
keyIdea.text: A script file stores code; the terminal and the python command run it in sequence and reproduce output.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › First Script
hello.py example
# This is my first Python script!
print("Hello, Cohortia learners!")
print("Python is fun!")
Save as my_first_script.py (or hello.py) and then run these commands in your terminal:
$ cd path/to/your/folder $ python my_first_script.py Hello, Cohortia learners! Python is fun!
If you see no output, check that you saved the file after edits and that your terminal is in the folder where the file lives. Use the ls or dir command to list files and confirm.
Scenario
You edited a file but the terminal shows the previous output. Most likely you did not save the file. Save and run again to see updated results.
Pro Tip
Keep a dedicated folder for projects, and cd into it before running scripts to avoid confusion about file locations.
Key Takeaway

Edit, save, change into the folder, and run with python filename.py to execute your script and see reproducible output.

screens.title: Interactive mode vs Script mode
screens.narratorSegment: Interactive mode and script mode serve different purposes and are complementary. Interactive mode is immediate and ephemeral: you type an expression and the interpreter shows the result; nothing is saved automatically. Use it to test small ideas, learn syntax, and inspect values. Script mode is persistent and repeatable: your commands are saved in a dot P Y file file and the interpreter runs everything in sequence when you ask it to. Use scripts when you want to keep a program, share it, or produce repeatable output. A concrete contrast: in the REPL you might try a single print call to check string formatting. In script mode you place multiple print calls or function definitions into a file so others can run the same program. A common misconception is to treat the REPL as a substitute for structured testing; because it doesn’t save state across sessions, tests belong in scripts. Key takeaway: experiment in the REPL, move proven lines into a script to preserve and run them repeatedly. Interactive mode vs Script mode means use the repl for exploration and scripts for preservation and repetition.. In practical terms, when to use the repl and when to write a file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Interactive vs Script
Interactive Mode (REPL)
  • Immediate evaluation and feedback.
  • Great for experimenting and quick calculations.
  • Session is ephemeral; actions are not saved to a file automatically.
>>> 2 + 2 4
Script Mode
  • Code is saved in a .py file and re-runnable.
  • Use scripts for programs that require multiple lines or need to be shared.
  • Run with python filename.py from the terminal.
# my_script.py print("Line one") print("Line two")
Misconception
The REPL is a substitute for saving code. It is not. Use it for testing, then transfer working code into scripts.
Key Takeaway
Experiment interactively, then save the final sequence as a script for reproducibility.

screens.title: Understanding SyntaxError
screens.narratorSegment: A SyntaxError occurs when the code violates Python’s grammatical rules. The interpreter cannot parse the statement because something is missing or misplaced, such as a missing closing parenthesis or an incorrect punctuation mark. For example, typing the print function without a closing parenthesis will produce a SyntaxError. The interpreter often points to the approximate location of the problem and may indicate that the file ended unexpectedly. To fix SyntaxError, read the message carefully, look at the line referenced, and check for common mistakes like missing parentheses, unmatched quotes, or incorrect indentation. A useful concrete workflow is to re-open the file, locate the line shown in the error, correct the punctuation, save, and re-run the script. A common misconception is that SyntaxError messages are cryptic; while sometimes terse, they reliably point you to the location to inspect. Over time you will recognize frequent patterns and fix them quickly. Final question to consider: when you see a SyntaxError, did you recently edit the file without saving? Always save before rerunning. Understanding SyntaxError means read the error location, correct punctuation or indentation, save, and re-run to confirm the fix.. In practical terms, what it means and how to fix it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › SyntaxError
What is a SyntaxError?

An error raised when Python cannot parse your code due to incorrect punctuation, unmatched quotes, missing parentheses, or similar grammar issues.

print("Welcome to Cohortia"
The interpreter will indicate a SyntaxError and often the line number or near the end-of-file where it expected more tokens. Inspect the referenced line closely.
Fixing steps
  1. Read the error message and note the line number.
  2. Open the file and check punctuation, quotes, and parentheses on that line.
  3. Save the file and run it again to confirm the error is gone.
Key Takeaway
SyntaxError messages point to grammar problems. Fix the punctuation and save before re-running.

screens.title: Understanding NameError
screens.narratorSegment: A NameError happens when you refer to a variable or function that the interpreter does not recognize. This usually occurs because of a typo, a missing definition, or a scope issue. For example, calling a function name spelled incorrectly, such as using pint instead of the print function, will raise a NameError. To fix a NameError, check for typographical errors first, then ensure the variable or function is defined before it is used. If the item should come from another module or file, confirm you performed the necessary import. A concrete diagnostic sequence is: read the message to find the undefined name, search your code for where it should have been defined or assigned, correct any typos, and rerun the script. A common misconception is that NameError always means the language is missing a built-in; often it simply signals a small typo. Ending question: before you run a script, did you define every name you call? That check prevents many NameError surprises. Understanding NameError means check spelling, definition order, and imports to resolve nameerror occurrences.. In practical terms, when python doesn't recognize a name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › NameError
What is a NameError?

Raised when code references a name that hasn't been defined in the current scope or was misspelled.

pint("Hello") # typo: 'pint' is not defined
Fix by correcting the name to print and re-running. If the name should have been set earlier in the code, ensure that line executed before the reference.
Debug checklist
  • Check for typos in the name.
  • Ensure the variable or function was defined before use.
  • Confirm necessary imports are present.
Key Takeaway
NameError usually signals a small typo or an undefined variable. Fix the name or the definition order and try again.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › pip
What is pip?

pip installs and manages external Python packages. It usually installs with Python, but you should verify it now.

$ pip --version pip 23.0.1 from ... (python 3.x)
If pip returns an error, ensure your Python installation completed and that pip is on PATH. Sometimes using pip3 instead of pip is appropriate on systems with multiple Python versions.
Why verify now?
Many later lessons require packages. Verifying pip now prevents interruptions later when you need to install a library quickly.
Key Takeaway
Confirm pip works so future package installs run smoothly. If it fails, re-check PATH or reinstall Python with pip enabled.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this short course you will learn how to install Python, interact with the interpreter, and run your first program. We start with the practical step of getting a trusted installer and making sure the operating system can find Python by adding it to PATH. Then you will try the interactive interpreter, called the REPL, to get immediate feedback and verify basic expressions and the print function. Finally you will create and run a small script file to see how script mode differs from interactive mode. Along the way I’ll show you common starter errors like a missing parenthesis or a misspelled function name and how to read the interpreter’s messages to fix them. A concrete example you will use is creating hello dot P Y file that prints two lines to the terminal and running it with the python command. This matters because a correct installation and basic workflow let you move from experimenting to building programs reliably. As you follow along, notice the commands and the error messages, and ask yourself: after installing, can I run python and pip from any directory? That ability is the most important indicator your setup is ready.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical, verifiable skills. First, you will be able to install Python and ensure the operating system can invoke it from any folder. This matters because a correct install is the foundation for running code and installing packages. Second, you will be able to explain what the Python interpreter is and use interactive mode to experiment quickly. Interactive mode helps you test ideas before committing them to a file. Third, you will write, save, and execute a simple Python script file from the terminal so you can move from experiments to reproducible runs. Finally, you will recognize and fix common startup errors such as a missing parenthesis or a misspelled function name. For each objective you will see a short demonstration and a small milestone you can check off, so you have concrete evidence of skill growth. These four outcomes prepare you to move on to variables, data types, and simple programs with confidence.

This chapter pairs concrete steps with short drills so you can verify each skill. You will practice installing Python and then immediately run two checks: python --version and pip --version. Those commands confirm both interpreter and package installer are available. Next you’ll enter the interactive interpreter to evaluate small expressions like simple arithmetic and call the print function to produce visible output. That immediate feedback is the drill for interactive mode. For script mode you will create a small file named my_first_script dot P Y file containing two print calls, save it to a folder, then navigate there and run it with the python command. Each drill ends with a simple pass/fail check: did you see the expected output? If not, the troubleshooting card guides you to re-check PATH, spelling, or missing parentheses. These short, repeatable steps build confidence and make setup failures easy to diagnose.

Installing Python is the first technical step and a common source of friction for beginners. The installer provides the Python executable and pip, the package installer. It is important to use the official installer mentioned in this chapter to avoid altered distributions. One particularly critical option on Windows is the checkbox to add Python to PATH. PATH is an operating-system environment list of folders that the terminal searches for executables. When Python is added to PATH you can type the python command from any folder and the interpreter will launch. Without that setting you may see a "command not found" or similar error, which means the system cannot locate the python program. A concrete example: after installation you will run python --version and expect a version string. If you see an error, re-run the installer and enable adding to PATH, or update the PATH environment variable manually. A common misconception is that installation always 'just works'; in fact, small checkbox choices matter. Key takeaway: confirm install with python --version and pip --version before moving on — these two checks prove your environment can run code and install packages.

The Python interpreter is the executable that reads your Python statements, translates them into operations, and performs them. Think of the interpreter as a translator that reads each line you write and does what you ask. There are two common ways to use the interpreter: interactive mode and script mode. In interactive mode you type a line and the interpreter responds immediately; this is ideal for testing ideas and learning syntax. In script mode you save a sequence of commands into a dot P Y file file and ask the interpreter to run the whole file from top to bottom. A concrete example of the interpreter in action is entering the REPL and typing a simple arithmetic expression; the interpreter evaluates it and returns the result. A common misconception is to confuse the interpreter with an editor: the interpreter executes code, while an editor simply stores it. To confirm the interpreter is available, run python --version. If the command prints the version, the interpreter is ready. Now consider how you will use interactive mode to experiment before writing scripts: that flow saves time when learning new concepts.

The interactive Read-Eval-Print Loop, or REPL, is where you type a Python expression and the interpreter evaluates it immediately. This is an ideal environment when you want to confirm syntax or test a small idea. To enter interactive mode type python or Python three in the terminal and press Enter. You will see the >>> prompt. At that prompt you can type arithmetic like 5 * 7 and press Enter to get the result. You can also call the print function to display text. For example, calling the print function with a greeting shows that the interpreter outputs strings correctly. When you are done, exit the REPL by calling exit() or using the platform-specific shortcut, such as Ctrl+D on Mac O S and Linux, or Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows. A common misconception is that work typed into the REPL is automatically saved; it is not. Use the REPL to experiment and then move the tested lines into a script file to preserve your work. Try a short sequence: start Python, compute a quick calculation, print a message, and then exit. That flow builds confidence and confirms the interpreter executes code as expected.

Writing your first script turns interactive trials into a reproducible program. Open a simple text editor and create a file named hello dot P Y file. Inside the file put two lines that call the print function to display messages. Save the file in a folder you can find easily, for example a projects folder or the Desktop. Then open your terminal and navigate to that folder using the cd command. Once you are in the correct folder, run the script by typing python hello dot P Y file or Python three hello dot P Y file depending on your system. You will see the two lines printed in order. A concrete script example from this chapter prints a friendly greeting and a short sentence about Python being fun. A common misconception is to expect the editor to run the file automatically; you must invoke the interpreter from the terminal. If the output does not appear, confirm you saved the file and that you are in the same directory. This simple flow — edit, save, cd, run — is a foundational loop you will repeat often.

Interactive mode and script mode serve different purposes and are complementary. Interactive mode is immediate and ephemeral: you type an expression and the interpreter shows the result; nothing is saved automatically. Use it to test small ideas, learn syntax, and inspect values. Script mode is persistent and repeatable: your commands are saved in a dot P Y file file and the interpreter runs everything in sequence when you ask it to. Use scripts when you want to keep a program, share it, or produce repeatable output. A concrete contrast: in the REPL you might try a single print call to check string formatting. In script mode you place multiple print calls or function definitions into a file so others can run the same program. A common misconception is to treat the REPL as a substitute for structured testing; because it doesn’t save state across sessions, tests belong in scripts. Key takeaway: experiment in the REPL, move proven lines into a script to preserve and run them repeatedly. Interactive mode vs Script mode means use the repl for exploration and scripts for preservation and repetition.. In practical terms, when to use the repl and when to write a file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A SyntaxError occurs when the code violates Python’s grammatical rules. The interpreter cannot parse the statement because something is missing or misplaced, such as a missing closing parenthesis or an incorrect punctuation mark. For example, typing the print function without a closing parenthesis will produce a SyntaxError. The interpreter often points to the approximate location of the problem and may indicate that the file ended unexpectedly. To fix SyntaxError, read the message carefully, look at the line referenced, and check for common mistakes like missing parentheses, unmatched quotes, or incorrect indentation. A useful concrete workflow is to re-open the file, locate the line shown in the error, correct the punctuation, save, and re-run the script. A common misconception is that SyntaxError messages are cryptic; while sometimes terse, they reliably point you to the location to inspect. Over time you will recognize frequent patterns and fix them quickly. Final question to consider: when you see a SyntaxError, did you recently edit the file without saving? Always save before rerunning. Understanding SyntaxError means read the error location, correct punctuation or indentation, save, and re-run to confirm the fix.. In practical terms, what it means and how to fix it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A NameError happens when you refer to a variable or function that the interpreter does not recognize. This usually occurs because of a typo, a missing definition, or a scope issue. For example, calling a function name spelled incorrectly, such as using pint instead of the print function, will raise a NameError. To fix a NameError, check for typographical errors first, then ensure the variable or function is defined before it is used. If the item should come from another module or file, confirm you performed the necessary import. A concrete diagnostic sequence is: read the message to find the undefined name, search your code for where it should have been defined or assigned, correct any typos, and rerun the script. A common misconception is that NameError always means the language is missing a built-in; often it simply signals a small typo. Ending question: before you run a script, did you define every name you call? That check prevents many NameError surprises. Understanding NameError means check spelling, definition order, and imports to resolve nameerror occurrences.. In practical terms, when python doesn't recognize a name. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
